Sustainability Isn't a Project You Finish

What UCLA's own power plant, underground tunnels, and native landscaping taught me about dreaming at the scale of decades.

EssayJanuary 2, 20262 min read
#Sustainability#UCLAAnderson

There's a quote I once heard: "If you reach all your dreams in this lifetime, you probably didn't dream big enough." Every time I hear leaders in sustainability speak, that thought comes back to me.

Listening to Nurit Katz talk about UCLA's work, I realized something. This isn't about small fixes. It's about dreaming at the scale of decades.

Did you know there are miles of underground tunnels carrying steam and chilled water across campus every single day? UCLA runs its own power plant, and captures waste heat to heat and cool buildings. The campus can disconnect from the grid and keep a hospital running during a blackout. Electric buses are being tested to charge while driving, through coils embedded under a campus road.

And then there's the part that really stayed with me. It's not just energy. It's ecology. Rethinking landscaping to use native plants. Reducing certain pesticides because they harm owls higher up the food chain. Paying attention to pollinators. That level of detail surprised me.

Not just big infrastructure decisions, but small, thoughtful choices that ripple through an ecosystem. Sustainability isn't a project you finish. It's long-term thinking. It's building systems someone else will inherit and improve. Maybe that's what dreaming big really looks like.
